title: Concurrency in Python: queues, coordination and deadlocks
seriesTitle: Python: threading, the GIL and asyncio
seriesDescription: Threads, locks, the GIL, concurrent.futures, asyncio, queues and classic drills. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: queue.Queue and its relatives, iteration safety, Event, Barrier, Semaphore, lock ordering, asyncio.Queue across threads and dumping thread stacks.
source: Python docs: queue, threading, asyncio, faulthandler; py-spy README; Real Python; GeeksforGeeks

questions.prompt: An empty queue.Queue named q is shared by several threads. What does q.get_nowait() do?

options.text: It raises queue.Empty immediately.
options.why: Correct: the non-blocking get signals "nothing there" with an exception (verified by running it).

options.text: It returns None immediately.
options.why: None is not used as an empty marker; a real item could even be None.

options.text: It blocks until another thread puts an item.
options.why: That is q.get() with the default block=True.

options.text: It waits one second and then returns None.
options.why: There is no default one second wait.

questions.explanation: get() blocks, get(timeout=t) raises Empty after t seconds, get_nowait() raises Empty at once. The put side mirrors it with queue.Full.

questions.prompt: Seven threads each call wait() once on the same new threading.Barrier(3). How many of them are still blocked after everything that can happen has happened?
questions.explanation: The barrier trips for every group of 3: two groups (6 threads) pass, and the seventh waits for two partners that never arrive (verified by running it). A Barrier is reusable, unlike a one-shot Event.

questions.prompt: A threading.Semaphore(2) is acquired once and then released twice. After that, how many consecutive acquire(blocking=False) calls succeed?
questions.explanation: Start 2, acquire leaves 1, two releases give 3, so three non-blocking acquires succeed and the fourth fails (verified). Semaphore does not remember who acquired; BoundedSemaphore would raise ValueError on the extra release.

questions.prompt: queue.Queue is thread-safe: several threads can call put() and get() on it without any extra locking.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: Queue does its own locking internally, which is why it is the standard hand-off between threads.

options.text: False
options.why: The class is built for multiple producers and consumers and needs no external lock.

questions.explanation: It is not safe across processes (use multiprocessing.Queue) and not meant for coroutines (use asyncio.Queue).

questions.prompt: Because of the GIL, looping over a dict in one thread while another thread adds new keys is always safe.

options.text: True
options.why: The GIL makes single operations atomic, but a loop is many steps.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the loop can fail with RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration (verified).

questions.explanation: Iterate over a snapshot such as list(d.items()), or guard the loop and the writers with the same Lock.

questions.prompt: Match each queue class with its behaviour.

right.text: First in, first out, thread-safe, optionally bounded
Last in, first out, a thread-safe stack
Always returns the smallest item first (usually priority, item tuples)
Unbounded FIFO with a very small API: no maxsize, no task_done
FIFO for coroutines on one event loop, not safe for use from other threads
Silently drops the oldest item when full

questions.explanation: Pick the class by who consumes: threads use queue.*, coroutines use asyncio.Queue. SimpleQueue is also reentrant, so it is safe in signal handlers and __del__ methods.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

lst = [1, 2, 3]
visited = []
for x in lst:
    visited.append(x)
    if x == 1: lst.append(99)
print(visited)

What is printed?

options.text: [1, 2, 3, 99], because the loop sees the appended element
options.why: Correct: a list iterator reads the live list by index, so growth is visible (verified by running it).

options.text: [1, 2, 3], because the loop works on a snapshot taken at the start
options.why: Snapshots are what you get from list(lst), not from iterating the list itself.

options.text: A RuntimeError, because a list may not change size while iterating
options.why: That error is raised for dicts and sets, not lists.

options.text: It never ends, because 99 is appended again on every pass
options.why: The append happens only when x equals 1, which occurs once.

questions.explanation: Lists silently misbehave when mutated during iteration, dicts raise, and neither is made safe by the GIL. Iterate over a copy when other code may mutate the collection.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentences about threading synchronisers.
questions.text: An {1} blocks waiters until set() is called and can be cleared and reused. A {2} makes a fixed number of threads wait for each other. A {3} limits how many threads hold permits at once.
questions.explanation: Condition adds wait/notify on a predicate, and Timer runs a function after a delay. Python has no CountDownLatch; use Event plus a counter, or join the threads.

questions.prompt: Write Python that starts 3 threading.Thread workers (each running do_work) and makes the main thread wait until all 3 have finished.

checks.label: creates Thread objects with a target
uses a loop or list for the 3 workers

questions.explanation: Start all threads before joining any, otherwise the workers run one after another. A ThreadPoolExecutor in a with block is the tidier equivalent. Join returns even if a worker failed, so check results separately.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Iterating over a shared dict while another thread inserts keys can raise RuntimeError even though each single dict operation is atomic.
questions.reason: A dict remembers the insertion order of its keys.

whys.a: R is true, but it says nothing about why concurrent modification breaks a loop.
whys.b: Correct: both true, but R is unrelated; the loop spans many separate operations and the dict can change size between steps.
whys.c: R is true (dicts keep insertion order since 3.7), so option c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true (verified by running it), so option d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Atomic operations do not compose. Copy with list(d) before looping, or hold a lock for the whole loop and for every writer.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: A worker thread may call asyncio.Queue.put_nowait() directly to hand items to coroutines.
questions.reason: asyncio.Queue is designed for coroutines on a single event loop and is documented as not thread-safe.

whys.a: A is false, so the pair cannot be a valid explanation.
whys.b: A is false, so option b is wrong.
whys.c: A is false, so option c (A true) is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: R is true and A is false. From another thread use loop.call_soon_threadsafe(q.put_nowait, item) or asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe.

questions.explanation: queue.Queue is for threads, asyncio.Queue for coroutines. Bridging needs call_soon_threadsafe.

questions.prompt: A Python worker process hangs in production and you must see what each thread is doing without restarting or modifying it. Which command does that?

options.text: py-spy dump --pid <pid>, attaching from outside
options.why: Correct: py-spy samples the process from outside and prints each thread's current Python stack.

options.text: jstack <pid>, the dump tool of another runtime
options.why: jstack reads another runtime's threads and cannot see Python frames.

options.text: kill -9 <pid> and then read the stack traces
options.why: SIGKILL ends the process and destroys the evidence.

options.text: python -m pdb --attach <pid> to step through it
options.why: pdb launches scripts; it cannot attach to a running process by pid.

questions.explanation: py-spy needs ptrace permission (often sudo, or CAP_SYS_PTRACE in containers). Alternatives: faulthandler.dump_traceback registered on a signal, or --native for C frames.

questions.prompt: Write an async Python function limited(sem, url) that waits for an asyncio.Semaphore before awaiting fetch(url) and returns the result, so at most N fetches run at once.

checks.label: uses the semaphore (async with or acquire)

questions.explanation: async with releases the permit even if fetch raises. In threads the same idea uses threading.Semaphore with a plain with statement.

questions.prompt: A worker thread must run step() repeatedly, once per second, until another thread asks it to stop. Given stop = threading.Event(), write the worker loop so that the stop request is noticed promptly, not after a full second.

checks.label: loops while the event is not set
waits on the event instead of sleeping

questions.explanation: Event.wait(timeout) sleeps like time.sleep but wakes at once when stop.set() is called. Threads cannot be killed from outside, so cooperative flags like this are the standard shutdown mechanism.

questions.prompt: Class Account has attributes id, balance and lock (a threading.Lock). Write transfer(src, dst, amount) so that two opposite transfers (A to B and B to A) can never deadlock, by always acquiring the lock of the account with the smaller id first.

checks.label: orders the two accounts by id

questions.model:
def transfer(src, dst, amount):
    first, second = sorted((src, dst), key=lambda a: a.id)
    with first.lock:
        with second.lock:
            src.balance -= amount
            dst.balance += amount
questions.explanation: A global lock order removes circular wait. Verified to finish with two opposite-direction threads. If ids can tie, add a tie-breaker; a src is dst transfer needs an RLock or a special case.

questions.prompt: From inside a Python process you want every thread stack printed when you send it the signal SIGUSR1, without extra packages. Which standard-library module does that?

options.text: tracemalloc, by starting it before the hang happens
options.why: tracemalloc tracks memory allocations, not thread stacks.

options.text: The faulthandler module, via register(SIGUSR1)
options.why: Correct: it writes all thread tracebacks to stderr when the signal arrives, even if the interpreter is stuck in a lock wait.

options.text: pdb, by attaching it to the running process id
options.why: pdb cannot attach to a running process by pid.

options.text: gc, by calling gc.get_objects() on the signal
options.why: That lists objects, it does not show where threads are executing.

questions.explanation: faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(timeout) is a watchdog variant. Externally, py-spy dump --pid does the same without touching the code.

questions.prompt: A queue.Queue with maxsize=2 is full. Match each call with what it does.

right.text: Blocks until a consumer makes room
Waits up to a second, then raises queue.Full
Never blocks, because there is no capacity limit

questions.explanation: put has the same four shapes as get: block, no wait, timeout, and the unbounded SimpleQueue. No standard queue overwrites old items; collections.deque(maxlen=n) does that.
